title: Installing Packages
text:
Installing a package is something you only need to do once per computer (much like installing RStudio itself only once). In most cases, you only need to give the package’s name to the install.packages() function. The following code installs the psych package.
## Install one package
install.packages("psych")
If you want to install more than one package at once, use the c() function to combine several package names into a single call.
## Install two packages at once
install.packages(c("mice", "lavaan"))
That’s it — those two patterns cover the vast majority of package installs you’ll ever need to do.

title: Installing Packages
text:
Common Errors
A few things commonly trip people up the first time they install a package:

Misspelling the package name. install.packages("ggplot") (missing the 2) will fail, because the package is actually called ggplot2. R can’t guess what you meant, so double-check the spelling against the package’s documentation or CRAN page.
Forgetting the quotes. install.packages(psych) (without quotes) tells R to look for an object called psych, not a package name, and will produce an error. Package names passed to install.packages() must be character strings, wrapped in quotes.
No internet connection. install.packages() needs to download the package, so it will fail (often with a fairly cryptic error) if you’re offline.







Practice



Use the install.packages() function to install the following packages in the default location.

ggplot2
dplyr
haven


 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "haven"))












Optional / Going Further: Repositories, Development Versions, and Library Locations



Everything above covers what you need for day-to-day work. This box covers a few more advanced topics you can come back to later if you ever need them.
Where packages come from. By default, install.packages() downloads packages from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). This is a global network of servers (“mirrors”) that each host a complete copy of all published R packages.RStudio automatically picks a sensible default mirror, so you don’t normally need to specify one. If you ever want to set one explicitly, you can do so via the repos argument.

## Explicitly specify a CRAN mirror
install.packages(c("lattice", "gridExtra"), repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

Other repositories. Occasionally, a package you need lives outside CRAN. Some other popular repositories include Bioconductor (specialized bioinformatics packages) and R-Universe.
Installing development versions. Package developers often share in-progress work on code-hosting platforms like GitHub. The remotes package lets you install directly from a GitHub repository, which sometimes gets you bug fixes or new features before they reach CRAN.

## Install the development version of the mice package from GitHub
remotes::install_github("amices/mice")

Choosing a library location. R usually figures out on its own where to install packages, prompting you if it needs a different location (e.g. because you lack write permission somewhere). You can also specify this explicitly with the lib argument.

## Install into a specific, non-default directory
install.packages("mvtnorm", lib = "../software")

title: Help File Sections
text: R help files can contain diverse information: some are only a few lines long while others contain dozens of pages of information. Not all R help files include all possible sections, but there are a few core sections that tend to show up pretty consistently due to their general usefulness. Below, we’ll walk through those sections using the documentation for the arrange() function (from the dplyr package) as a concrete example.

title: Help File Sections
text:
Description

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Description

  arrange() orders the rows of a data frame by the values of selected columns.
  
    Unlike other dplyr verbs, arrange() largely ignores grouping; you need to explicitly mention grouping
    variables (or use  .by_group = TRUE) in order to group by them, and functions of variables are
    evaluated once per data frame, not once per group.
  





As the name implies, the Description section provides a brief, human-readable description of the functions purpose.

title: Help File Sections
text:
Usage

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Usage

  arrange(.data, ..., .by_group = FALSE)

## S3 method for class 'data.frame'
arrange(.data, ..., .by_group = FALSE, .locale = NULL)





The Usage section shows the fully parameterized function call. In other words, how to call the function. In particular, this section provides several crucial pieces of information.

The name used to call the function
The name of all the function arguments
The order of the function arguments
Any default values defined for function arguments

title: Help File Sections
text:
Arguments

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Arguments

  







.data
A data frame, data frame extension (e.g. a tibble), or a lazy data frame (e.g. from dbplyr or dtplyr). See Methods, below, for more details.


...
<data-masking> Variables, or functions of variables. Use desc() to sort a variable in descending order.


.by_group
If TRUE, will sort first by grouping variable. Applies togrouped data frames only.


.locale
The locale to sort character vectors in.

If NULL, the default, uses the "C" locale unless the dplyr.legacy_locale global option escape hatch is active. See the dplyr-locale help page for more details.
If a single string from stringi::stri_locale_list() is supplied, then this will be used as the locale to sort with. For example, "en" will sort with the American English locale. This requires the stringi package.
If "C" is supplied, then character vectors will always be sorted in the C locale. This does not require stringi and is often much faster than supplying a locale identifier.

The C locale is not the same as English locales, such as "en", particularly when it comes to data containing a mix of upper and lower case letters. This is explained in more detail on the locale help page under the ⁠Default locale⁠ section.









The Arguments section briefly explains each function argument. As you might suspect, the arguments section will probably be the one you reference most frequently since the information contained herein explains the purpose or each function argument and what type of values you are able to specify for each argument.

title: Help File Sections
text:
Details

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Details

  Missing values

  Unlike base sorting with sort(), NA are:

  
    
       always sorted to the end for local data, even when wrapped with desc().
    
    
       treated differently for remote data, depending on the backend.
    
  





The Details section expands on the information listed in the Arguments section to provide additional details of function arguments or the functions behavior

title: Help File Sections
text:
Value

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Value

  An object of the same type as .data. The output has the following properties:

  
    
       All rows appear in the output, but (usually) in a different place.
    
    
       Columns are not modified.
    
    
       Groups are not modified.
    
    
       Data frame attributes are preserved.
    
  





The Value section describes the type of object returned by the function.

title: Help File Sections
text:
Examples

R: Order rows using column values
  
  
  
  
  
  



  Examples

  arrange(mtcars, cyl, disp)
arrange(mtcars, desc(disp))

# grouped arrange ignores groups
by_cyl <- mtcars %>% group_by(cyl)
by_cyl %>% arrange(desc(wt))
# Unless you specifically ask:
by_cyl %>% arrange(desc(wt), .by_group = TRUE)

# use embracing when wrapping in a function;
# see ?rlang::args_data_masking for more details
tidy_eval_arrange <- function(.data, var) {
  .data %>%
    arrange({{ var }})
}
tidy_eval_arrange(mtcars, mpg)

# Use `across()` or `pick()` to select columns with tidy-select
iris %>% arrange(pick(starts_with("Sepal")))
iris %>% arrange(across(starts_with("Sepal"), desc))





The Examples section contains executable R code that demonstrates the function’s primary use-cases.

title: Independent Task
text:
You’ve now practiced opening help files, reading their sections, and using them to figure out argument order and default values with some guidance along the way. This page works the same muscle, but without the step-by-step scaffolding. You’re on your own this time, the same way you would be when you encounter an unfamiliar function in your own work.






Independent Task



The strsplit() function is part of Base R, so it’s available without loading any additional packages. You haven’t used it anywhere in this module. Using only its help file, answer the following:

What does strsplit() do, in one sentence?
What are its arguments called, and in what order are they specified?
Does any argument have a default value? If so, what is it?
Write a function call that splits the text "apple,banana,cherry" into its three individual words, using the comma as the split point.


 Question Solution


Open strsplit()’s help file however you’d like, and work through the four questions above before checking the solution.



?strsplit







strsplit
R Documentation





Split the Elements of a Character Vector

Description

Split the elements of a character vector x into substrings
according to the matches to substring split within them.



Usage

strsplit(x, split, fixed = FALSE, perl = FALSE, useBytes = FALSE)



Arguments





x
character vector, each element of which is to be split. Other inputs, including a factor, will give an error.


split
character vector (or object which can be coerced to such) containing regular expression(s) (unless fixed = TRUE) to use for splitting. If empty matches occur, in particular if split has length 0, x is split into single characters. If split has length greater than 1, it is re-cycled along x.


fixed
logical. If TRUE match split exactly, otherwise use regular expressions. Has priority over perl.


perl
logical. Should Perl-compatible regexps be used?


useBytes
logical. If TRUE the matching is done byte-by-byte rather than character-by-character, and inputs with marked encodings are not converted. This is forced (with a warning) if any input is found which is marked as "bytes" (see Encoding).






Details

Argument split will be coerced to character, so
you will see uses with split = NULL to mean
split = character(0), including in the examples below.

Note that splitting into single characters can be done via
split = character(0) or split = ""; the two are
equivalent.  The definition of ‘character’ here depends on the
locale: in a single-byte locale it is a byte, and in a multi-byte
locale it is the unit represented by a ‘wide character’ (almost
always a Unicode code point).

A missing value of split does not split the corresponding
element(s) of x at all.

The algorithm applied to each input string is

    repeat {
        if the string is empty
            break.
        if there is a match
            add the string to the left of the match to the output.
            remove the match and all to the left of it.
        else
            add the string to the output.
            break.
    }

Note that this means that if there is a match at the beginning of a
(non-empty) string, the first element of the output is "", but
if there is a match at the end of the string, the output is the same
as with the match removed.

Note also that if there is an empty match at the beginning of a non-empty
string, the first character is returned and the algorithm continues with
the rest of the string.  This needs to be kept in mind when designing the
regular expressions.  For example, when looking for a word boundary
followed by a letter ("[[:<:]]" with perl = TRUE), one can
disallow a match at the beginning of a string (via "(?!^)[[:<:]]").

Invalid inputs in the current locale are warned about up to 5 times.



Value

A list of the same length as x, the i-th element of which
contains the vector of splits of x[i].

If any element of x or split is declared to be in UTF-8
(see Encoding), all non-ASCII character strings in the
result will be in UTF-8 and have their encoding declared as UTF-8.
(This also holds if any element is declared to be Latin-1 except in a
Latin-1 locale.)
For perl = TRUE, useBytes = FALSE all non-ASCII strings in a
multibyte locale are translated to UTF-8.

If any element of x or split is marked as "bytes"
(see Encoding), all non-ASCII character strings created by
the splitting in the result will be marked as "bytes", but encoding
of the resulting character strings not split is unspecified (may be
"bytes" or the original).  If no element of x or
split is marked as "bytes", but useBytes = TRUE, even
the encoding of the resulting character strings created by splitting is
unspecified (may be "bytes" or "unknown", possibly invalid
in the current encoding).  Mixed use of "bytes" and other marked
encodings is discouraged, but if still desired one may use
iconv to re-encode the result e.g.  to UTF-8 with suitably
substituted invalid bytes.



Warning

An all too common mis-usage is to pass unnamed arguments which are then
matched to one or more of fixed,
perl and useBytes.  So it is good
practice to name all  the arguments.



See Also

paste for the reverse,
grep and sub for string search and
manipulation; also nchar, substr,
startsWith, and endsWith.

‘regular expression’ for the details of the pattern
specification.

Option PCRE_use_JIT controls the details when perl = TRUE.



Examples

noquote(strsplit("A text I want to display with spaces", NULL)[[1]])

x <- c(as = "asfef", qu = "qwerty", "yuiop[", "b", "stuff.blah.yech")
# split x on the letter e
strsplit(x, "e")

unlist(strsplit("a.b.c", "."))
## [1] "" "" "" "" ""
## Note that 'split' is a regexp!
## If you really want to split on '.', use
unlist(strsplit("a.b.c", "[.]"))
## [1] "a" "b" "c"
## or
unlist(strsplit("a.b.c", ".", fixed = TRUE))

## a useful function: rev() for strings
strReverse <- function(x)
        sapply(lapply(strsplit(x, NULL), rev), paste, collapse = "")
strReverse(c("abc", "Statistics"))

## get the first names of the members of R-core
a <- readLines(file.path(R.home("doc"),"AUTHORS"))[-(1:8)]
a <- a[(0:2)-length(a)]
(a <- sub(" .*","", a))
# and reverse them
strReverse(a)

## Note that final empty strings are not produced:
strsplit(paste(c("", "a", ""), collapse="#"), split="#")[[1]]
# [1] ""  "a"
## and also an empty string is only produced before a definite match:
strsplit("", " ")[[1]]    # character(0)
strsplit(" ", " ")[[1]]   # [1] ""









strsplit() splits the elements of a character vector into substrings, according to a specified splitting character or pattern.
Its arguments are x, split, fixed, perl, and useBytes, specified in that order.
fixed, perl, and useBytes all default to FALSE. x and split have no defaults — you must supply them.
::: {.cell layout-align=“center”}
strsplit("apple,banana,cherry", split = ",")
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
[[1]]
[1] "apple"  "banana" "cherry"
::: :::

title: Accessing Help Files
text:
The simplest way to access a function’s help file is to prepend the function name (without parentheses) with the ? character. The following code will pull up the documentation for the lm() function.








Reading



R4DS 8: Getting Help



?lm

You can achieve the same effect by providing the function name to the help() function.

help(lm)
help("lm")

A function’s help file comes from the package that provides the function. So, you typically cannot access the help file for a function until you’ve loaded the package that provides that function.
For example, the following code will produce an error because we’re trying to access the documentation for arrange(), but we haven’t yet loaded the dplyr package that provides the arrange() function.

?arrange

No documentation for 'arrange' in specified packages and libraries:
you could try '??arrange'


We can still access the help files for functions provided by an unloaded package, though. We just have to tell R which package provides the function (and, hence, where to look for the help file). To do so, either use the namespace resolution operator, ::, or provide a value for the package argument in the help() function.

The vector() function is provided by the base package, which is loaded every time you start R. So, you should be able to access the help file without loading any additional packages.


According to the Usage section of vector()’s documentation,

The vector() function takes 2 arguments: mode and length.
The default argument for mode is “logical”.


?vector







vector
R Documentation









A vector in R is either an atomic vector i.e., one of the atomic
types, see ‘Details’, or of type (typeof) or mode
list or expression.

vector produces a ‘simple’ vector of the given length and
mode, where a ‘simple’ vector has no attribute, i.e., fulfills
is.null(attributes(.)).

as.vector, a generic, attempts to coerce its argument into a
vector of mode mode (the default is to coerce to whichever
vector mode is most convenient): if the result is atomic
(is.atomic), all attributes are removed.
For mode="any", see ‘Details’.

is.vector(x) returns TRUE if x is a vector of the
specified mode having no attributes other than names.
For mode="any", see ‘Details’.






vector(mode = "logical", length = 0)
as.vector(x, mode = "any")
is.vector(x, mode = "any")









mode
character string naming an atomic mode or "list" or "expression" or (except for vector) "any". Currently, is.vector() allows any type (see typeof) for mode, and when mode is not "any", is.vector(x, mode) is almost the same as typeof(x) == mode.


length
a non-negative integer specifying the desired length. For a long vector, i.e., length > .Machine$integer.max, it has to be of type "double". Supplying an argument of length other than one is an error.


x
an R object.








The atomic modes are "logical", "integer",
"numeric" (synonym "double"), "complex",
"character" and "raw".

title: General Rules
text:
General Rules for Calling Functions

A function call always follows the pattern function_name(arguments).
Every opening parenthesis needs a matching closing parenthesis.
Function names (and argument names) are case-sensitive: mean() and Mean() are not the same thing.
Arguments are separated by commas.
You can name arguments (round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)) or rely on their order (round(3.14159, 2)), but if you skip a name, the order matters.
Text values must be wrapped in quotes ("like this"); object names and numbers are not.

Putting It All Together






Practice



Using what you’ve learned across this tutorial, write a single R expression that:

Creates a vector of the numbers 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, and 42, called nums.
Calculates the mean of nums, rounded to 1 decimal place.


 Interactive Editor Hint Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


You’ll need three functions here: one to build the vector, one to average it, and one to round the result. You’ve used all three earlier in this tutorial.



nums <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
round(mean(nums), 1)

[1] 18


Notice that this solution nests one function call inside another: mean(nums) is calculated first, and its result is immediately passed as the input to round(). You’ll see this pattern constantly once you get comfortable with it.

title: Understanding Arguments
text:
What Are Arguments?
On the last page, you already changed the inputs to round() and saw the output change. Those inputs have a name: arguments. Arguments are simply the inputs you give to a function, written inside its parentheses.

function_name(arguments)

Most R functions accept more than one argument, and each argument has its own name. You specify argument values by writing a comma-separated list of name = value pairs between the parentheses of the function call.

round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14


Do: run the two lines of code.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
See: both lines produce the same result.
Explain: if you supply argument values in the order the function expects them, you don’t have to write out the argument names. Both round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2) and round(3.14159, 2) tell R exactly the same thing — the second version is just a shortcut.






Practice: Predict, Then Run



The mean() function accepts an argument called trim, which excludes a proportion of the most extreme values before averaging. Predict what each line below will print.

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 100)
mean(x)
mean(x, trim = 0.2)


 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 100)
mean(x)

[1] 22

mean(x, trim = 0.2)

[1] 3


mean(x) averages all five values, including the outlier 100, which pulls the average up substantially. mean(x, trim = 0.2) first removes the most extreme 20% of values on each end before averaging, giving a result that’s much closer to the “typical” value in the data.

title: Understanding Arguments
section: A Note on Named vs. Positional Arguments
text:
A Note on Named vs. Positional Arguments
You don’t always need to write out an argument’s name, but if you skip the name, R will assume you’re supplying the arguments in the order the function expects. Mixing these two styles is common and perfectly fine, as long as you keep the ordering rules straight:

If you name all your arguments, you can put them in any order.
If you name none of your arguments, you must put them in the function’s expected order.
If you name some, the unnamed ones must still come first, in the expected order.

We’ll come back to exactly how you find out a function’s expected argument order and default values once we cover documentation later in this module. For now, it’s enough to recognize that arguments have names, and that those names matter.

Creating Objects
We create objects by ‘assigning’ values to names via the ‘assignment’ operator, <-. The following code assigns the values 7, 2.5, and "foo" to the objects x, y, and z, respectively.
Do: Run the following code.

Assignment is a silent operation: it creates a new object in the current R session but doesn’t print anything. This behavior can be confusing, so it’s worth taking a moment to internalize the distinction. Assigning a value and printing a value are two separate steps.

Notice that x still equals 7 after the last line, even though we just computed x - 1. Doing arithmetic with an object does not change the value stored in that object, R only updates an object’s value when you explicitly re-assign it with <-.

title: R Objects & Assignment
text:
Copies, Not Renames
We can also create new objects by assigning them the values of existing objects.
The following code creates a new object, w, that takes the value of the existing object z. When we print the value of w, you can see that it has the same value as z.

w <- z
w

[1] 5

z

[1] 5


When we create w above, we are not replacing z with w: we’re making a copy of z and calling that copy w. So, both w and z are still available. In almost all cases, R will copy objects during assignment. This behavior is good to keep in mind when you’re working with larger datasets: you can quickly flood your memory with unnecessary copies of your data, if you’re not careful.

Notice that R never “sees” the letters x, y, z as text. Instead, it looks up whatever value is currently stored in each object and calculates with that. If you’d assigned different values to x, y, or z, these same three lines of code would produce entirely different answers without you changing a single character of the arithmetic itself. This is one of the most useful properties of programming: the same logic can be reused with different data.

Powers & Roots
We use the caret character, ^, to specify exponents. For example, the following code will square and cube the value of y.

The sqrt() function returns the square root of its argument (i.e., the value we specify inside the parentheses). The following code calculates the square root of y.

section: Why Bother With Objects at All?
text:
Why Bother With Objects at All?
You might wonder why we don’t just write 7 + 2.5 directly instead of y + x. For a single calculation, writing the numbers directly is perfectly fine. But once your calculations get longer, or once you want to reuse a value multiple times, giving that value a name (an object) makes your code far easier to read, reuse, and fix.
We’ll return to objects properly, including how to create them, a little later in this tutorial. For now, the important idea is just that R objects behave like named “slots” that hold a value, and arithmetic on those objects uses whatever value is stored inside.

text:
Almost all the commands you’ve seen so far have been some sort of mathematical operation (e.g., adding, dividing, computing the natural logarithm), but R can do much more for us. Logical comparisons are one particularly useful class of operations, in which we test compare objects to test logical conditions. We can test many flavors of logical conditions in R. Logical tests return a logical value as the result. A logical value is TRUE whenever the tested condition is satisfied and FALSE when the tested condition is not satisfied.

title: Logical Comparisons
text:
Equality
The simplest logical test is an equality check. To check if two objects are equal, we use the equality operator, ==.

1 == 1

"a" == "a"

[1] TRUE

"foo" == "bar"

[1] FALSE








Common Mistakes



Notice that the equality test operator, ==, is two equals signs. Remember that a single equals sign is one of the possible assignment operators. You cannot use a single equals sign to do a logical comparison.

2 = 3

Error in `2 = 3`:
! invalid (do_set) left-hand side to assignment


Mixing up == and = is one of the most common beginner mistakes (and experienced user typos) in R.

title: Order of Operations
text:
When parsing your commands, R will, mostly, scan each line of code from left to right and apply each mathematical operation according to the usual PEMDAS ordering (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Do: run both lines below and compare the results.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
See: the two lines produce different answers, even though they use the same three numbers and the same three operators.
Explain:

In the first line, R first divides x by z, and then adds y to the result.
In the second line, the parentheses force R to first add x to y, and only then divide the result by z.

Parentheses are your most reliable tool for controlling order of operations. When in doubt, add parentheses. They never hurt, and they make your intent explicit both to R and to anyone (including future-you) reading the code.

In the first case, we’re raising y to the power of \(\frac{1}{2}\) — which is the same as taking a square root.

[1] 3.5


In the second case, R applies the exponent (^) before the division, so it first raises y to the power of 1 (which does nothing) and only then divides the result by 2. The exponent operator has higher precedence than division, so it’s applied first even though it appears “attached” to the 1 rather than the whole expression.

arrange(.data, ..., .by_group = FALSE, .locale = NULL)

  Arguments

  







.data
A data frame, data frame extension (e.g. a tibble), or a lazy data frame (e.g. from dbplyr or dtplyr). See Methods, below, for more details.


...
<data-masking> Variables, or functions of variables. Use desc() to sort a variable in descending order.


.by_group
If TRUE, will sort first by grouping variable. Applies togrouped data frames only.


.locale
The locale to sort character vectors in.

If NULL, the default, uses the "C" locale unless the dplyr.legacy_locale global option escape hatch is active. See the dplyr-locale help page for more details.
If a single string from stringi::stri_locale_list() is supplied, then this will be used as the locale to sort with. For example, "en" will sort with the American English locale. This requires the stringi package.
If "C" is supplied, then character vectors will always be sorted in the C locale. This does not require stringi and is often much faster than supplying a locale identifier.

The C locale is not the same as English locales, such as "en", particularly when it comes to data containing a mix of upper and lower case letters. This is explained in more detail on the locale help page under the ⁠Default locale⁠ section.

  Missing values

  Unlike base sorting with sort(), NA are:

  
    
       always sorted to the end for local data, even when wrapped with desc().
    
    
       treated differently for remote data, depending on the backend.
    
  

  Value

  An object of the same type as .data. The output has the following properties:

  
    
       All rows appear in the output, but (usually) in a different place.
    
    
       Columns are not modified.
    
    
       Groups are not modified.
    
    
       Data frame attributes are preserved.
    
  

  Methods

  
    This function is a generic, which means that packages can provide implementations (methods) for
    other classes. See the documentation of individual methods for extra arguments and differences in behaviour.
  
  The following methods are currently available in loaded packages: no methods found.

  See Also

  
    Other single table verbs: 
    filter(),
    mutate(),
    reframe(),
    rename(),
    select(),
    slice(),
    summarise()
  

  Examples

  arrange(mtcars, cyl, disp)
arrange(mtcars, desc(disp))

# grouped arrange ignores groups
by_cyl <- mtcars %>% group_by(cyl)
by_cyl %>% arrange(desc(wt))
# Unless you specifically ask:
by_cyl %>% arrange(desc(wt), .by_group = TRUE)

# use embracing when wrapping in a function;
# see ?rlang::args_data_masking for more details
tidy_eval_arrange <- function(.data, var) {
  .data %>%
    arrange({{ var }})
}
tidy_eval_arrange(mtcars, mpg)

# Use `across()` or `pick()` to select columns with tidy-select
iris %>% arrange(pick(starts_with("Sepal")))
iris %>% arrange(across(starts_with("Sepal"), desc))

title: Common Mistakes
text: Everyone runs into the same handful of errors when they’re getting started with functions. Recognizing them quickly will save you a lot of frustration. Each example below is broken on purpose, try to spot the problem before reading the explanation.

title: Common Mistakes
text:
Mistake 1: Forgetting a Closing Parenthesis

round(3.14159, 2

Error in parse(text = input): <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
1: round(3.14159, 2
   ^


Explain: every opening parenthesis needs a matching closing parenthesis. R will often show a + prompt (instead of an error) and appear to “hang” while it waits for you to finish the expression. If that happens, you’re almost always just missing a closing ).

title: Common Mistakes
text:
Mistake 2: Misspelling a Function Name

maen(1:5)

Error in `maen()`:
! could not find function "maen"


Explain: R is case-sensitive and doesn’t guess at typos. maen() doesn’t exist, so R tells you it “could not find function.” Double-check your spelling (and capitalization) whenever you see this error.

title: Common Mistakes
text:
Mistake 3: Misnaming an Argument

round(3.14159, digit = 2)

[1] 3.14


Explain: the round() function expects an argument called digits (plural), not digit. R doesn’t recognize digit as a valid argument name for round(), so it raises an error rather than guessing what you meant.

title: Common Mistakes
text:
Mistake 4: Forgetting Quotes Around Text

x <- hello

Error:
! object 'hello' not found


Explain: without quotation marks, R assumes hello is the name of an existing object, and complains that it can’t find one. To create a piece of text (a character string), you must wrap it in quotes: x <- "hello".

title: What Is a Function?
text:
A function is a small, reusable piece of code that someone else has already written for you, packaged up under a short name so that you can use it without needing to know (or care) exactly how it works internally.
Think of a function like a kitchen appliance. A blender doesn’t require you to understand its motor or wiring. You put ingredients in, press a button, and get a smoothie out. R functions work the same way:

Input — you give the function some data to work with.
Operation — the function does something to that data (behind the scenes).
Output — the function gives you back a result.


Input → Function (does the operation) → Output

title: What Is a Function?
text:
How Functions Are Named
You will almost always be able to quickly identify the functions in a piece of R code by the fixed pattern: FUNCTION_NAME(). That is, an R function is called by writing the function’s name followed immediately by an opening parenthesis. The following list shows some commonly encountered R functions.

mean()
sum()
c()
round()
sqrt()

So, any time you see a word immediately followed by parentheses in R code, you’ve found a function call.






Practice: Spot the Functions



Which of the following lines contain a function call? Predict your answer, then check it against the solution.

 Question Solution



x <- 7
y <- sqrt(49)
z <- x + 2
w <- round(3.14159, 2)




x <- 7 — No function call. Just assignment of a literal number.
y <- sqrt(49) — Yes, sqrt() is a function call.
z <- x + 2 — No function call. Just arithmetic on an object.
w <- round(3.14159, 2) — Yes, round() is a function call.

title: What Is a Function?
text:
Why This Matters
Almost every useful thing you’ll do in R, from simple calculations to complex statistical models, involves calling functions. Getting comfortable spotting them, and understanding the input → operation → output pattern, is the single most important conceptual step in this tutorial. Everything else builds on it.






Going Further: Functions as Mathematical Formulas



If you’re comfortable with algebra, it can help to know that R functions work in essentially the same way as mathematical functions. Feel free to skip this box entirely if it doesn’t help you.
The following equation represents a linear function of \(x\).
\[
f(x) = 1.5 + 2x
\]
For any value of \(x\) that we provide as input, \(f(x)\) first multiplies that value by 2 and then adds 1.5 to the resulting product. So, if we let \(x = 3\), we get \(f(3) = 7.5\).
\[
\begin{align*}
f(3) &= 1.5 + 2 \times 3\\
&= 7.5
\end{align*}
\]
The mean() function we used to motivate these ideas operates through the same conceptual process. If we let \(n\) represent the number of values in \(x\), we could notate the mathematical definition of the mean() function as follows.
\[
\begin{align}
f(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_i
\end{align}
\tag{1}\]
Doing the analogous calculation in R would look like the following.

a <- 1:5
mean(a)

[1] 3


In most of your R analyses, you won’t need to worry about defining the functions you use: that work has already been done by the developers who wrote the packages you’re using. You will usually only have to worry about preparing the input, calling an appropriate function, and processing the function’s output.

title: Argument Order & Defaults
text: As we alluded to in the Understanding Arguments page, the Usage section of an R documentation file provides two very important pieces of information about a function’s arguments.

title: Argument Order & Defaults
text:
Argument Ordering
When you call an R function, you do not have to explicitly write out the argument names, if you supply the argument values in the order that the arguments are specified in the function definition. That’s a mouthful, so let’s look at the matrix() function for a concrete example.








matrix
R Documentation





Matrices

Description

matrix creates a matrix from the given set of values.

as.matrix attempts to turn its argument into a matrix.

is.matrix tests if its argument is a (strict) matrix.



Usage

matrix(data = NA, nrow = 1, ncol = 1, byrow = FALSE,
       dimnames = NULL)

as.matrix(x, ...)
## S3 method for class 'data.frame'
as.matrix(x, rownames.force = NA, ...)

is.matrix(x)



Arguments





data
an optional data vector (including a list or expression vector). Non-atomic classed R objects are coerced by as.vector and all attributes discarded.


nrow
the desired number of rows.


ncol
the desired number of columns.


byrow
logical. If FALSE (the default) the matrix is filled by columns, otherwise the matrix is filled by rows.


dimnames
a dimnames attribute for the matrix: NULL or a list of length 2 giving the row and column names respectively. An empty list is treated as NULL, and a list of length one as row names. The list can be named, and the list names will be used as names for the dimensions.


x
an R object.


...
additional arguments to be passed to or from methods.


rownames.force
logical indicating if the resulting matrix should have character (rather than NULL) rownames. The default, NA, uses NULL rownames if the data frame has ‘automatic’ row.names or for a zero-row data frame.











The usage section of matrix()’s help file tells use that the function takes five arguments:

data
nrow
ncol
byrow
dimnames

Furthermore, we see that these five arguments are specified in the order shown above.
If we explicitly write out the names for all the arguments in our function call, we can specify the argument values in any order. Hence, the following three lines will produce equivalent results, for example.

matrix(data = 1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = FALSE, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6

matrix(nrow = 3, ncol = 2, data = 1:6,byrow = FALSE, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6

matrix(byrow = FALSE, data = 1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6


If we provide the argument values in the order they are specified in the function definition, we do not need to write out the argument names. So, the following function call will produce the same result as the three above.

matrix(1:6, 3, 2, FALSE, NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6


We can also mix these two approaches, but we have to provide all unnamed argument values first, and provide them in the correct order. The following function calls will also produce the same results as above.

matrix(1:6, 3, 2, FALSE, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6

matrix(1:6, 3, 2, byrow = FALSE, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6

matrix(1:6, 3, dimnames = NULL, byrow = FALSE, ncol = 2)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    4
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    3    6


We cannot, however, switch the order of any unnamed argument values. The following code will not reproduce the matrix created above.

## Flip the 'nrow' and 'ncol' arguments
matrix(1:6, 2, 3, FALSE, dimnames = NULL)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

title: Argument Order & Defaults
text:
Default Values
When the Usage section shows a value assigned to a function argument, the value shown is the default value for that function argument. For the matrix() function, all five arguments have default values.

data = NA
nrow = 1
ncol = 1
byrow = FALSE
dimnames = NULL

When a function argument has a defined default value, we do not need to specify a value for that argument in our function call: if we don’t provide an argument value, the argument takes the default value shown in the documentation.
So, we could technically call the matrix() function without specifying any arguments.

matrix()

     [,1]
[1,]   NA


Though, the results are rather boring. Since our function call is entirely parameterized by the default arguments, we get a \(1 \times 1\) matrix containing a single missing datum.
In practice, we will almost always specify some argument values, but we will frequently accept some of the default values, as well. The following is a typical example of calling the matrix() function.

matrix(1:12, nrow = 4)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    5    9
[2,]    2    6   10
[3,]    3    7   11
[4,]    4    8   12


In the above function call, I’ve employed two common shortcuts:

I didn’t name the first argument.
I only specified values for the two arguments that I wanted to adjust.

What is the default value of the by argument?
Write a call to seq() that generates the sequence 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 — using the by argument explicitly, but relying on default values for anything else.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


You’ll need to give seq() a starting value (from), an ending value (to), and a step size (by). Check the Usage section to confirm the argument names and their default values.


According to the Arguments section of seq()’s help file (?seq), by’s default value is (to - from)/(length.out - 1) — in other words, it has no simple fixed default; R calculates a sensible step size automatically if you don’t provide one. To generate our specific sequence, we supply by explicitly:

title: Add-On Packages
text:
What Is a Package?
A package is simply a collection of functions (plus, sometimes, data and documentation) that someone else has written and bundled up for others to use — the exact same idea as the individual functions you’ve already been calling, just packaged together in a reusable, installable unit. Just like you don’t need to know how mean() is implemented internally to use it, you don’t need to know how a package’s functions work internally to use them either.
The following list shows a few common data-analysis tasks and some packages that provide relevant functions for each.

Treating missing data using multiple imputation

mice
Amelia
mi

Structural equation modeling

lavaan
OpenMx

Multilevel regression modeling

lme4
nlme

For all but the most trivial data processing, manipulation, and visualization, the tidyverse packages are virtually obligatory.

Over the rest of this tutorial, you’ll learn the two steps every package requires before you can use it: installing it (once) and loading it (every time you start a new R session and want to use it).

title: Loading Packages
text:
Once you’ve installed a package, you’re nearly ready to use its functions, but there’s still one step left: you must load the package into your active R session.
The following code produces an error because we’re trying to use the ggplot(), aes(), and geom_boxplot() functions provided by the ggplot2 package, without having loaded that package first.
ggplot(iris, aes(Species, Petal.Length)) + geom_boxplot()

Error in `ggplot()`:
! could not find function "ggplot"
An R package is really just a small piece of software. Like any other software, you only need to install it once (just like you only need to install RStudio once), but you need to load it every time you start a new R session and want to use it (just like you need to open RStudio every time you want to use it).
We load packages with the library() function.
library(dplyr)
library() can only load one package at a time, so call it once per package if you need more than one.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
Running the code below should now produce a simple plot, since we’ve loaded ggplot2 before trying to use the functions it provides.

title: Loading Packages
text:
Common Errors

Using a package’s functions before loading it. This is exactly the error you saw at the top of this page. It’s the single most common package-related mistake. If R tells you it “could not find function,” check whether you’ve loaded the package that provides it.
Trying to load a package you haven’t installed. library() will error with something like “there is no package called…” if the package isn’t installed yet. Installing and loading are two separate steps. You need to install a package (once) before you can ever load it.
Misspelling or mis-capitalizing the package name. Package names are case-sensitive, just like function names. library(Dplyr) will fail even though library(dplyr) works fine.

title: Fundamental Interactions
text:
Order of Operations
When parsing your commands, R will, mostly, scan each line of code from left to right and apply each mathematical operation according to the usual PEMDAS ordering (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction).
Run the following two lines of code and compare their results.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Notice that the two lines produce different answers, even though they use the same three numbers and the same three operators. Why?

In the first line, R first divides 4 by 2, and then adds 3 to the result.
In the second line, the parentheses force R to first add 3 to 4, and only then divide the result by 2.

Parentheses are your most reliable tool for controlling order of operations. When in doubt, add parentheses. They never hurt, and they make your intent explicit both to R and to anyone (including future-you) reading the code.






Practice

 Question Solution

[1] 3

9^1/2

[1] 4.5





9^(1/2)

[1] 3

sqrt(9)

[1] 3


In the first case, we’re raising 9 to the power of \(\frac{1}{2}\), which is the same as taking its square root.

9^1/2

[1] 4.5

9 / 2

[1] 4.5


In the second case, R applies the exponent (^) operator before the division operator (/). So, we first raise 9 to the power of 1 (which does nothing), and then we divide the result by 2. In the end, we’ve just used some convoluted code to dived 9 by 2.





Now that you’re aware of R’s rules for operator precedence, let’s revisit the birth day/month problem from above.

title: R Objects & Assignment
section: Why Bother with Objects at All?
text:
Why Bother with Objects at All?
You might wonder why we don’t just write 7 + 2.5 directly instead of y + x. For a single calculation, writing the numbers directly is perfectly fine. But once your calculations get longer, or once you want to reuse a value multiple times, giving that value a name (an object) makes your code far easier to read, reuse, and fix.
We’ll return to objects properly, including how to create them, a little later in this tutorial. For now, the important idea is just that R objects behave like named “slots” that hold a value, and arithmetic on those objects uses whatever value is stored inside.

title: R Objects & Assignment
text:
Assigning Existing Objects
In real-world data analysis, we rarely create objects by directly assigning single numbers. Typically, we create objects by manipulating existing objects and assigning the manipulated version to a new name. Fortunately, R is perfectly happy to create new objects by assigning them the values of existing objects.
The following code creates a new object, w, that takes the value of the existing object z. When we print the value of w, you can see that it has the same value as z.

w <- z
w

[1] 5

z

[1] 5








Important



When we create w in the code above, we are not replacing z with w: we’re making a copy of z and naming that copy w. So, both w and z are still available (otherwise we wouldn’t be able to print the value of z). In almost all cases, R will copy objects during assignment. This behavior is good to keep in mind as you progress to more complicated projects. If you’re not careful, your environment can quickly become cluttered with unused copies of old objects.








Practice



Given the objects defined above (x <- 2.5, y <- 7, z <- 5), predict the value of each expression before running it.

z + y
z * x
z - y


 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

[1] 12

z * x

[1] 12.5

z - y

[1] -2


Notice that R does not interpret the letters x, y, z as text. Instead, it uses whatever value is currently stored in each object when doing the calculations. If you assign different values to x, y, or z, these same three lines would produce entirely different answers. Try it for yourself.
In the following code block, replace the ? with a new value for z, and rerun the expressions.

Notice how each line now produces a different result, even though you didn’t change anything about the expressions, themselves. This paradigm is one of the most useful properties of programmatic data analysis. By changing the values stored in the relevant objects (e.g., by loading a different dataset), you can reuse the same code to re-run the same calculation on different data.











Common Mistakes



Even though we name objects with words, R has different ways of handling named objects and character strings.

We use quotation marks to denote a character string.
We don’t quote object names.

If we run foo <- "bar", foo is an object that stores the character string "bar". We need to be careful with what we quote: foo and "foo" are completely different entities. Most quotation-based mistakes fall into one of two classes.
Mistake 1: We forget the quotation marks when trying to define a character string.

# We want to assign the character string "bar" to the object foo
foo <- bar

Error:
! object 'bar' not found


Since we didn’t quote the value on the right-hand-side of the assignment operator, R will try to find an object called bar and assign its contents to foo. Since, bar doesn’t exist, we get an error.
Mistake 2: We quote an objects name.

alice <- 42
bob <- 1984

# We want to add the values stored in the objects alice an bob
alice + "bob"

Error in `alice + "bob"`:
! non-numeric argument to binary operator


In this case, we should have written alice + bob. Both alice and bob exist as objects that store numeric values, but "bob" is just a character string that has no relation to the object bob. So, R tries to add the value stored in alice (i.e., 42) to the string-literal "bob" and fails.

title: R Objects & Assignment
text:
Why Bother?
You might wonder why we don’t just write 7 + 2.5 directly instead of first assigning 7 to y, then assigning 2.5 to x, and finally computing y + x. For a single calculation, writing the numbers directly is perfectly fine, but not when your calculations get longer and more complex. In real-world projects, you will need to reuse certain data values multiple times. So, storing those values as named objects makes your code far easier to read, reuse, and fix.

title: Logical Comparisons
text:
Greater-Than & Less-Than
We can also check the usual greater-than/less-than conditions with >, <, >=, <=.

# Is y greater than x?
y > x

[1] FALSE

# Is y greater than or equal to x?
y >= x

[1] FALSE

# Is y less than x?
y < x  # less than

[1] TRUE

# Is y less than or equal to x?
y <= x # less than or equal to

[1] TRUE

[1] FALSE

y <= w

[1] TRUE


y and w store the same value, so:

y > w and y < w are both FALSE, since neither is strictly greater or less than the other.
y >= w and y <= w are both TRUE, since “greater than or equal to” and “less than or equal to” are satisfied whenever the values are equal.

title: Environments
text:
The Global Environment
The global environment is the highest-level environment that R maintains. This environment contains all of the objects you define in your R session. Whenever you create a new object (as you’ve been doing throughout this module), that object lives in the global environment.






Note



Since the global environment is the one you’ll interact with most frequently, its often treated as the default environment when economizing language (i.e., being lazy).

In these tutorials, whenever we refer to “the environment”, “your current environment”, “your R session”, or some variation of those terms, we’re talking about the global environment.
The Environment tab in RStudio shows the contents of the global environment, by default.
The interactions described below all interface with the global environment, by default.
